study.title: Let us go to the house of the LORD
study.intro: Psalm 122 is the joy of arrival. The pilgrim who began far away in Psalm 120 and looked to the hills in Psalm 121 now stands inside Jerusalem's gates. He remembers the gladness of the invitation, admires the city, and then prays for its peace. It is a song about the delight of worshiping together and caring for the community of God's people.
study.context: Headed 'of David', this psalm celebrates Jerusalem, which David made the capital and the place of the ark. Three times a year the tribes of Israel traveled there for the feasts (Deuteronomy 16:16). The city held the house of the LORD and the royal courts where justice was given. The name Jerusalem sounds like shalom, peace, and the psalm plays on that word in its prayer.
study.peopleNote: Attributed to David, who brought the ark to Jerusalem and made it the center of Israel's worship. The speaker is a pilgrim among brothers and friends. God is never portrayed as a human figure in planned art.

verses.title: Glad to go up
verses.heading: Let us go to the house of the LORD
verses.meaning: 'I was glad when they said to me, “Let us go to the house of the LORD.”' The joy starts with an invitation. Friends or neighbors came and said, 'Let's go worship together,' and the singer's heart leaped. Worship here is not a lonely duty but a shared delight. There is something special about being invited and about going with others to meet with God. Sometimes the best gift we can give someone is that same invitation.
verses.context: Pilgrims traveled in large groups of family and neighbors, as Luke 2:44 shows when Jesus' parents assumed He was among their relatives. Hebrews 10:25 urges believers not to neglect meeting together, and Isaiah 2:3 pictures nations saying, 'Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD.'
explore: House of the LORD
The tabernacle and later the temple in Jerusalem, where God's presence was especially known.
Pilgrimage
A journey to a holy place for worship, made by Israel three times a year for the feasts.
verses.reflect: Who invited you to worship or to know God? Who could you invite?
verses.alt: A group of villagers with walking staffs setting out together on a road.

verses.title: Standing in the gates
verses.heading: Our feet are standing in your gates
verses.meaning: 'Our feet are standing in your gates, O Jerusalem.' After days of walking, the pilgrims finally arrive. Their tired feet are now planted inside the city of God. You can almost feel the relief and wonder. The long journey is over, and they are where they longed to be. This verse captures the joy of reaching a goal and the sense of belonging in God's presence with His people.
verses.context: City gates were the busy center of public life, where people met and judges sat (Ruth 4:1). Psalm 84:10 says a day in God's courts is better than a thousand elsewhere. Hebrews 12:22 speaks of believers coming to the heavenly Jerusalem.
explore: Gates
The fortified entrances of a walled city, also the place where business and court cases happened.
Jerusalem
The city David made Israel's capital, where the temple stood and the feasts were celebrated.
verses.reflect: What does it feel like to arrive somewhere you belong? How does that picture your life with God?
verses.alt: Travelers stepping through a great stone city gate into a crowded street.

verses.title: A city bound together
verses.heading: Built up as a city united
verses.meaning: 'Jerusalem is built up as a city united together,' The pilgrim admires the city itself. Its buildings are packed closely, wall joined to wall, solid and compact. But the description is also spiritual: Jerusalem is where scattered tribes become one people. The city's tight construction pictures the unity God wants for His people, many families and backgrounds joined together around one center of worship.
verses.context: Jerusalem was a compact hilltop city. Ephesians 2:21-22 describes believers as a building joined together into a holy temple, and Psalm 133:1 celebrates how good it is when brothers live together in unity.
explore: United together
Bound or joined closely, like stones fitted into a wall; a picture of togetherness.
Built up
Constructed and established, often with the sense of being made strong and complete.
verses.reflect: Where do you see God joining very different people together in your church or community?
verses.alt: Close-packed stone houses climbing a hillside within city walls.

verses.title: Where the tribes go up
verses.heading: To give thanks to the name of the LORD
verses.meaning: 'where the tribes go up, the tribes of the LORD, as a testimony for Israel, to give thanks to the name of the LORD.' This is why the city matters. All twelve tribes make the trip to Jerusalem because God commanded it. Their going up is a testimony, a public witness that they belong to the LORD. And the purpose of it all is thanksgiving. Worship is not just obligation; it is grateful people telling God's name.
verses.context: Deuteronomy 16:16 commanded all Israelite men to appear before the LORD three times a year. The tribes are called 'the tribes of the LORD' because they belong to Him. Psalm 100:4 calls worshipers to enter His gates with thanksgiving.
explore: Tribes
The twelve family groups of Israel, descended from the sons of Jacob.
Testimony
A witness or ordinance; here God's decree that His people gather, which also showed whose they were.
verses.reflect: What has God done this week that you can give thanks for by name?
verses.alt: Crowds of families climbing stone steps toward a temple courtyard.

verses.title: Thrones of justice
verses.heading: The thrones of the house of David
verses.meaning: 'For there the thrones of judgment stand, the thrones of the house of David.' Jerusalem was not only a place of worship but also the seat of government. David's royal family sat there to hear cases and give justice. Worship and justice belong together: the God who receives praise also cares deeply that people are treated rightly. The verse also points ahead to the greater Son of David, Jesus, who will judge with perfect fairness.
verses.context: Kings in Israel judged disputes, as Solomon did in 1 Kings 3:16-28. Isaiah 9:7 promises that the Messiah will sit on David's throne, upholding it with justice and righteousness. Luke 1:32 says Jesus will receive the throne of His father David.
explore: Thrones of judgment
Seats where rulers heard cases and gave legal decisions for the people.
House of David
David's royal family line, to whom God promised an everlasting kingdom in 2 Samuel 7.
verses.reflect: Why do you think God wants justice and worship to be found in the same place?
verses.alt: An empty carved stone seat in an open courtyard with morning light.

verses.title: Pray for its peace
verses.heading: Pray for the peace of Jerusalem
verses.meaning: 'Pray for the peace of Jerusalem: “May those who love you prosper.' Now the song becomes a prayer and a call to prayer. In Hebrew there is wordplay: pray for shalom (peace) for Yerushalayim, and may those who love you be secure. Loving God's people means praying for their well-being. Those who care for the community of faith find that their own lives are bound up in its blessing.
verses.context: Jeremiah 29:7 told exiles to seek the peace of the city where they lived and pray for it. Ephesians 6:18 urges prayer for all God's people. Psalm 51:18 asks God to do good to Zion and build Jerusalem's walls.
explore: Peace
Shalom, the deep wholeness, safety and well-being that God gives a people.
Prosper
To be secure and at rest; the Hebrew word suggests calm and safety more than wealth.
verses.reflect: Whose peace can you pray for today: your church, your city, or God's people far away?
verses.alt: A person kneeling in prayer on a rooftop overlooking a city at evening.

verses.title: Peace within the walls
verses.heading: Prosperity inside your fortresses
verses.meaning: 'May there be peace within your walls, and prosperity inside your fortresses.”' The prayer continues with protection in mind. Walls and fortresses guarded the city from enemies outside, but real peace has to live inside. A community can look strong from the outside and still be torn apart within. The pilgrim prays for both: safety from outside attack and harmony among the people who live and worship together.
verses.context: Nehemiah rebuilt Jerusalem's walls for protection (Nehemiah 2:17). Jesus wept over Jerusalem in Luke 19:42 because it did not recognize the things that make for peace, and Philippians 4:7 promises God's peace guarding hearts and minds.
explore: Walls
The defensive stone barriers around a city, a picture of protection and security.
Fortresses
Strong towers or citadels within a city where defenders could hold out against attack.
verses.reflect: What would real peace inside your home or church look like?
verses.alt: Strong city walls with towers glowing in late afternoon sun.

verses.title: For my brothers and friends
verses.heading: Peace be within you
verses.meaning: 'For the sake of my brothers and friends, I will say, “Peace be within you.”' Why pray for Jerusalem? Because the people the singer loves are there. His brothers and friends, the whole family of faith, live within those walls. Prayer for a community is really prayer for people with names and faces. Love moves us to bless others, and speaking peace over them is one of the simplest ways to do it.
verses.context: Jesus told His disciples to greet a house with 'Peace to this house' (Luke 10:5). Paul often opened letters with 'Grace and peace to you' (Romans 1:7). 1 John 4:21 says whoever loves God must also love his brother.
explore: Brothers
Fellow members of God's covenant family, not only blood relatives.
Peace be within you
A blessing spoken over others, wishing them God's wholeness and well-being.
verses.reflect: Who are the brothers and friends you can speak a blessing of peace over today?
verses.alt: Two friends embracing in greeting at a village doorway.

verses.title: For the house of God
verses.heading: I will seek your prosperity
verses.meaning: 'For the sake of the house of the LORD our God, I will seek your prosperity.' The deepest reason comes last. Jerusalem matters because God's house is there. The singer commits not only to pray but to seek the city's good, to act for it. Love for God leads to love for the place and people where He is worshiped. Today that means caring for the church, the people among whom God now dwells.
verses.context: Nehemiah 2:10 describes someone coming to seek the well-being of Israel. 1 Corinthians 3:16 says believers together are God's temple, and Galatians 6:10 urges doing good especially to the household of faith.
explore: Seek
To pursue actively, working toward something rather than only wishing for it.
Prosperity
Good and well-being in every sense, the flourishing of a community.
verses.reflect: What is one practical way you can seek the good of your church or faith community this week?
verses.alt: Workers repairing a temple courtyard wall with baskets of stones.
